opening.headline: The reason why answers to the same question vary and even non-existent sources appear is explained through three structures: token, context window, and stochastic generation.
body: You may have had the experience of asking the same question to generative AI twice and getting different answers, or receiving an answer with a plausible paper title and author, but when you searched, no such paper was found. This phenomenon is not a malfunction, but a feature of the way the model creates answers.

In this class, we will sequentially look at tokens, which are the units in which the model reads text, a context window that determines the amount that can be handled at once, a knowledge cutoff that indicates the learning point, and a generation method that probabilistically connects the next token. At the end, you will learn the framework for distinguishing the cause of incorrect answers through examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the meaning of tokens, context windows, and probabilistic generation in their own words.
You can distinguish whether hallucination originates from a knowledge cutoff, context limit, or generation method.
Describe the effects and limitations of sampling settings, such as temperature, on the variation of answers.
The reason why the model leans toward giving plausible answers rather than saying it doesn't know can be explained through the structure of learning and evaluation.

screens.title: Same question, different answer, no source.
screens.lead: First, let's look at a scene that many people actually experience. Read the situation below and think about what's strange.

visual.alt: A scene with two different answer cards to the same question and a third answer card with a non-existent paper citation.
labels: Please tell me the size of the domestic market

paragraphs: To find out the market size to include in the report, I asked the same question twice in the AI chat window. The first answer was about 3.2 trillion won, and the second answer was about 4.1 trillion won. The question didn't change a single letter, but the number changed.

When the same question was asked a third time, the answer this time was a quote from the '○○ Research Institute 2023' report. The title, year, and institution name were all complete. But when I searched, no such report existed.

All three answers were written in a confident and assertive tone. You can't tell which answer is correct just by looking at the tone of voice. The question for this class is this. Why does this happen and how can we determine where the cause is?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Are the different answers and the emergence of non-existent sources the same or different causes? By the end of the lesson, you will be able to answer this question yourself.

screens.outro: Now let’s get started by reflecting on your own experiences.

screens.title: Have you ever seen something similar?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever had a moment when you were embarrassed because you got different answers to the same question?
items.answer: This experience is very common. The reason the answer to the same question varies is not because the model breaks down in a different way each time, but because probability intervenes in the way the answer is created. In this lesson, we will see the structure in pictures.

items.prompt: Have you ever checked the source or figures later and found them wrong?
items.answer: OpenAI Help cites non-existent citations or studies, incorrect dates and definitions as typical forms of hallucination. Because the causes and responses vary depending on the type of error, in this class we will practice classifying errors by type.

items.prompt: At that time, what did you suspect: ‘what the model doesn’t know’ or ‘what I didn’t tell you enough’?
items.answer: At first, we usually move towards blaming the model or rewriting the question. However, the causes are divided into three areas: learning point, amount that can be stored at one time, and generation method. Knowing where to suspect determines how to check.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized our experience, let's start with the smallest unit of text that the model reads: the token.

screens.title: Token: The smallest unit of text through which the model reads text.
screens.lead: Select the arrows to move through each step as sentences turn into tokens and usage.

visual.alt: Flow illustration where sentences are divided into token chips followed by token number and cost.
labels: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
Calculate usage and costs based on inputs and outputs
One token ≒ 4 letters, 100 tokens ≒ 60 to 80 English words

steps.title: It starts with a sentence
steps.body: To a human being, 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.' is a sentence made up of nine words. However, the model does not read this sentence word for word or literally. The Gemini documentation explains that Gemini and other generative AI models process input and output in units called tokens.

steps.title: Divide into tokens
steps.body: The token may be a single letter, such as `z`, or a single word, such as `cat`. Long words are broken into multiple tokens. The process of dividing a sentence into tokens is called tokenization, and the collection of all tokens used by the model is called the vocabulary. Therefore, the boundaries of a word that a person feels may not match the boundaries of a token.

steps.title: Measure size by number of tokens
steps.body:
The standard presented in the document is that in the Gemini model, one token is approximately 4 letters, and 100 tokens correspond to 60 to 80 English words. These values ​​are approximate. You can tell how much the model is actually processing by measuring the length of the article in terms of tokens rather than characters or pages.

This estimate is based on the English text. In languages ​​other than English, such as Korean, even text with the same meaning tends to cost more tokens, and each tokenizer, which is a program that divides text into tokens, has different dividing methods, so the number of tokens for the same text varies depending on the model. One study reported that the number of tokens can vary by up to 15 times when translating the same content into multiple languages. Therefore, do not determine the limit or cost of Korean documents based on this estimate, but measure it directly using the token counting tool of the service you plan to use.

steps.title: Counts non-text input as well
steps.body: All inputs and outputs from the Gemini API are tokenized. In addition to text, non-text inputs such as image files are also counted as tokens. Therefore, it is difficult to estimate the size of a document containing many photos just by the number of characters.

steps.title: It becomes the standard for usage and cost.
steps.body: When billing is turned on, the cost of a Gemini API call is determined in part by the number of input and output tokens. Before sending a request, you can pre-count the number of tokens in the input with `count_tokens`, and the response contains `usage` information dividing the input, output, thoughts, cache, and tool usage tokens. A token is a common unit that measures both size and cost.

screens.outro: Now that we have a unit called a token, we move on to the context window, which is the space that contains this token.

ext.title: Petrov et al., Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages (NeurIPS 2023)

screens.title: Context Window and knowledge cutoff: Two Boundaries
screens.lead: Choose one of the two states and compare how the model's range of knowledge changes with the search tool turned on and off.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the context window bar on the left and the knowledge cutoff timeline on the right.
labels: Context window (combined limit of input + output)
After the reference date: unknown without tools
If search is turned on, it will be filled with web source links.

states.label: Search off
states.body:
The model only answers based on patterns contained in the training data. OpenAI help explains that the model is trained on data up to a certain point in time, and without tools, its responses will not reflect events after that point. This boundary is the knowledge cutoff.

The context window is a separate limitation. The context window is the limit on the number of tokens that input and output can use together in a single request. For example, Gemini 4 Argon has a combined input and output window of 1,048,576 tokens, and output at one time is up to the default 65,536 tokens. Some models, such as the Gemini 3 series, have separate input and output limits, so you need to check for each model.

Also note how the window is filled. The model itself does not remember previous conversations separately. Each time the conversation-continuing service sends a new question, it re-includes the previous conversation in the input and passes it to the model. Even if the service stores the conversation state on the server for you, the principle is the same: that content is included in the input read by the model. So the longer the conversation, the larger the input for each request and the faster the window fills.

Just because it's inside a window doesn't mean that all information is used with the same weight. One study reported a tendency for accuracy to drop noticeably in long inputs when the needed information was in the middle rather than at the beginning or end, and that the same trend was seen in models designed for long inputs.

In summary, when search is turned off, the specifications of yesterday's product cannot be found, no matter how large the window is. This is because the window is limited to the amount it can contain, and the base date is when learning is completed.

states.label: Search on
states.body:
When the search tool is turned on, the model can find current information on the web and give you a source-labeled answer. OpenAI help explains that you can access and cite real-time web sources by using search or deep research. The empty section after the base date is filled with the source link.

There are two ways to check if search is turned on: See if the search or deep research icon is turned on in the input field, and see if web sources are cited in the response. If the source is attached, it is a good idea to open the link directly to check whether the content matches the answer.

However, even if search is turned on, the limits of the context window remain the same. Because search results and conversations are all in the same window, earlier conditions may get pushed out in long conversations. Also, if access to the website is blocked or has a paid section, the model may not be able to retrieve the necessary information.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the two boundaries - the limit and the base date - let's look at how they are created, which is why the answer varies every time.

ext.title: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL)
Anthropic Messages API documentation (pass previous conversation turns as messages with each request)

screens.title: Probabilistic Generation: Why the Answers Change
screens.lead: Move the slider to see three different times when a sentence is created. Let's look at how the distribution of next token candidates changes at each time point.

visual.alt: A vertical chart that displays the next token candidate as a bar at each point in a sentence.
labels: Probability of next token being drawn

stops.body:
When asked, the model selects a candidate for the first token based on the learned pattern. There are several candidates, such as 'market', 'size', and 'recent', and none of them has a probability of 0. The candidate with the highest odds is often chosen, but not always.

OpenAI help explains that ChatGPT creates responses based on patterns in the training data. The starting point is not to find and read facts, but to continue speaking according to a pattern.

The already selected tokens change the distribution of the next candidates. If it continues to 'The size of the domestic market is about', there is a higher possibility that the number and unit will be selected next time. However, which number will come is only a plausible value from the learning pattern, not a fact found through search.

At this point, even if the candidates are narrowed down to two or three, probability is involved in the selection process, so if the same question is sent again, a different number may be selected. This is why it was divided into 3.2 trillion won and 4.1 trillion won in the first scene.

By joining the tokens one by one, the entire sentence is completed. A completed sentence reads smoothly and assertively, but its tone has nothing to do with whether the content is correct. The OpenAI help makes it clear that the model can express high confidence even in wrong answers.

Since it is a way to connect plausible sentences, quotations such as ‘○○ Research Institute 2023’ can be made into natural sentences. Hallucination is the phenomenon of making up citations, studies, and sources that do not exist, and it is the user's responsibility to verify the content.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the creation method, let's compare how the process of creating an answer differs depending on the type of model.

screens.title: Sampling and temperature: knobs for selecting candidate distributions
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to see what each setting changes when controlling how the next token is drawn. The explanation below the table also explains why the same input does not guarantee exactly the same output.

visual.alt: Three sets of bar graphs showing how the probability bar of the next token candidate changes when lowering and increasing temperature.

data.caption: Three settings that control how the next token is drawn
rows: temperature
Sharpen or flatten the probability distribution of candidate tokens
Candidates with higher probability are chosen more overwhelmingly and their answers become similar.
Even low-probability candidates have more chances to be selected, leading to more diverse answers.
top-p
The candidates with the highest probability are added in order, leaving only the candidates until the total reaches a set value and selecting from among them.
As the number of remaining candidates decreases, only safe choices are selected.
As the number of remaining candidates increases, even rare choices become candidates.
top-k
Only a certain number of candidates are selected in order of probability.
A value of 1 results in a greedy selection that always selects only the candidate with the highest probability.
As the range of candidates expands, a variety of expressions can emerge.
data.notes:
For example, suppose the next token candidates are 'about' 60 percent, 'approximately' 25 percent, 'total' 10 percent, and 'other' 5 percent. These figures are assumptions for illustrative purposes only. If you lower the temperature, the share of 'weak' becomes larger, and if you increase it, the shares of the four candidates become closer to each other. In either case, the process of probabilistically selecting one of the candidates remains the same. top-p is a proposed sampling method that maintains diversity while truncating low-probability tails.

The reason why the results are different even with the same input is because of this draw. In models that take sampled values, lower temperatures may reduce diversity, but they do not guarantee completely conclusive results. As of 2026-10, Claude Opus 4.7·4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 5.5, etc. may reject non-default sampling values, so you must check model/SDK support before sending the corresponding parameters. There is also analysis that the calculation order may vary depending on the size of the inference server processing multiple requests. Therefore, lowering the value reduces the deviation, but does not guarantee identical output down to the letters.

Lastly, these settings are not values ​​adjusted on the chat app screen, but values ​​specified in API calls. Depending on the model, the Gemini documentation indicates that even if this value is specified, it will be ignored, so first check whether the model you want to use receives the value.

screens.outro: Now that we know how to select candidates, let's look at the learning structure to see why the model leans toward giving plausible answers rather than saying it doesn't know.

ext.title: Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (top-p, nucleus sampling)
Gemini API prompt strategy document (temperature, topP, topK)
Thinking Machines Lab, Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference

screens.title: Why we make it up: Assumptions made by learning objectives and assessments.
screens.lead: Select the arrows to move through each step and follow how the model is created and how the evaluation method leads to guessing habits.

steps.title: Pre-training: Training to guess the next token
steps.body: The model is first trained to guess the next token by looking at the preceding tokens in a large text. In this process, you learn grammar, writing style, and many factual patterns. However, the goal of training is to come up with plausible next words, not just say verified facts.

steps.title: Follow-up adjustments: Refine to human preference
steps.body: A model that has only completed pre-training may not follow instructions well, so typically two stages of adjustment are added. This is the stage of additional learning using model answers written by people, and the stage of reinforcement learning based on preferences given by people by comparing multiple answers. The InstructGPT paper describes this approach, reporting that the tweaked model followed instructions better and gave people preferred answers.

steps.title: A place where the line between knowing and not knowing is blurred
steps.body: There are areas where the pattern to distinguish between correct and incorrect statements is weak, such as facts that appear only once or twice in the training data. Kalai et al.'s paper analyzes that in areas where the model cannot distinguish between correct and incorrect statements, such errors occur simply due to the statistical pressure of prior learning.

steps.title: Evaluations encourage speculation
steps.body: The same paper points out that many benchmarks only accept correct answers and no 'don't know' answers. In this grading method, those who answer questions they don't know are always at an advantage over those who leave them blank. When a model is refined for these assessments, it becomes more inclined to answer rather than say I don't know.

steps.title: Meaning for users
steps.body: So the model usually moves in the direction of the answer, and the tone may be confident, but that doesn't mean it's grounded. Instructions that allow you to say you don't know or require evidence are effective because they change the direction against this gradient. It's still up to the user to make sure the content is correct.

screens.outro: Now let's compare how the process of creating an answer differs depending on the type of model.

ext.title: Kalai et al., Why Language Models Hallucinate
Ouyang et al., Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)

screens.title: General model and inference model, multimodal input
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the differences when sending the same question to two types of models and the differences in input format.

visual.alt: A side-by-side illustration of the responses of a general model and an inference model to the same question, with a row of input type icons below them.

tabs.label: regular model
tabs.body:
When a normal model is asked a question, it immediately starts producing an answer. It's quick to respond and has a simple structure, making it ideal for requests that require one or two steps, such as summaries, translations, and simple classifications.

When the same question is asked to a general model, it is common for the response to come first with a conclusion followed by a short period of evidence. In cases where calculations require multiple steps or have overlapping conditions, the risk of making a mistake can be relatively high due to skipping intermediate steps.

tabs.label: inference model
tabs.body:
The inference model goes through an internal thinking phase before coming up with an answer. This is why it is advantageous for multi-step problems or problems with complicated conditions. When you send the same question, it takes longer to get a response, but the answer is often structured in stages.

The Gemini document reveals that tokens used in this way are also counted separately as `total_thought_tokens`. In other words, even if the visible answer is short, usage increases by the amount of tokens used internally. The inference model is suitable for difficult problems, and the general model is suitable for simple requests where a quick response is important.

tabs.label: Multimodal input
tabs.body:
Multimodal refers to the ability to receive input other than text. The Gemini API handles text as well as non-text input, such as image files, as tokens. The Claude documentation explains that the model supports text and image input.

Even if the input type is different, the principle of using the context window is the same. The more images you include, the more tokens are used, so the more pictures your document contains, the faster the window will fill.

tabs.label: Summary of differences
tabs.body:
The general model produces an answer right away and is suitable for quick and simple requests. The inference model has a thinking step before answering, which is advantageous for multi-step problems, but tokens spent on thinking are added to usage.

Both types are similar in that they probabilistically connect the next token. Therefore, even an inference model can create sources that do not exist, and the source of important information must be verified directly.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the model type and input type, let's break down the actual case by cause.

screens.title: Case Commentary 1: Answer mixed with made-up sources
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of disassembling answers mixed with made-up sources. Select the arrows and follow them step by step.

steps.title: case
steps.body: When I asked about the market size for the report, I got this answer. 'The domestic market size in 2023 was estimated at approximately 3.2 trillion won, and is expected to reach 4.5 trillion won in 2025 (Source: ○○ Research Institute, 2023).' The text is sleek and complete with year-by-year figures and citations. Now let's take a step-by-step look at how to check this answer.

steps.title: Step 1: Make sure search is turned on
steps.body: First, check whether the search or deep research icon is turned on in the input window. And make sure the response includes a link to the web source. These are the two verification methods that OpenAI Help guides you through. In this case, search was turned off and there were no links.

steps.title: Step 2: Determine if it was created from a pattern
steps.body: If there were no searches, the figures and citations would have been concatenated from learned patterns. It's just a natural combination of a plausible lab name, year, and growth rate, not something you read somewhere. The smoother the sentence, the easier it is to accept it without question, so you have to be more careful.

steps.title: Step 3: Check whether it is typical of hallucination
steps.body: OpenAI Help cites non-existent citations, studies, and sources as examples of hallucination. In this case, the quote '○○ Research Institute, 2023' fits exactly that type. The fact that there is a citation is not evidence, but rather a signal that you should check the citation yourself.

steps.title: Conclusion: Attach evidence or check directly
steps.body: The response is two-pronged. One is to turn on search or deep research and ask the same question again to receive an answer with a source attached. The other is to directly open the attached link and check whether the content matches the answer. As the help says, ChatGPT's answers are treated as drafts, not final sources, and important citations and figures are verified.

screens.outro: Now that we have solved one case, let us organize the causes into a three-pronged framework.

screens.title: Case commentary 2: Dividing the causes into three branches
screens.lead: Each row in the table is the result of decomposing one case. Read from top to bottom to find out which cause the case corresponds to, on what basis it is judged, and how to respond.

data.caption: Table classifying error cases by cause
rows: Case A: Misrepresenting the specifications of a recently announced product
knowledge cutoff
The event occurred after the end of the study period and there were no search tools or web sources.
Turn on search or deep research and open the source link to check.
Case B: Missing previously set conditions late in a long conversation
Context Limit

Conversations were re-entered in their entirety for each request, causing the window to fill up so the front part was pushed out, or even within the window, conditions placed in the middle of long input were underused.
Summarize the conditions and repeat them or move them to a new conversation.
Case C: Seamlessly creating non-existent citations
Creation method
In the process of plausibly connecting the following tokens, non-existent research and sources were created.
Open and check the source directly and do not use unfounded quotations.
data.notes:
A single error may have multiple causes. For example, in a long conversation asking about recent events, both reference date issues and window limit issues may arise. In this case, determine based on the evidence which is the main cause and apply the appropriate response first. The fact that the tone is assertive is no basis for accuracy in either cause.

After classification, response follows. If it's a base date issue, the tool will bring you up-to-date information. If it's a window limit issue, reduce the conversation or reiterate only the key terms. If there is a problem with the generation method, the model's answer is drafted and a human can check the basis. If you first divide the cause, you can decide where to start checking even if you experience the same error repeatedly. Read the table like a case card and match which row is closest to the error you experienced.

screens.outro: Now that we have a classification framework, we will finally summarize the entire content.

ext.title: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL)

screens.title: Combining three limitations into one scene
screens.lead: Read again to see how the concepts covered in this lesson explain the initial scene.

paragraphs: Let's go back to the first scene. The reason 3.2 trillion won and 4.1 trillion won came out in the same question is because of the generation method. The model probabilistically selects and concatenates the next token, so the sentence may be different each time. This is not an error, but a feature of how it works.

The appearance of the '○○ Research Institute 2023' citation also stems from the same method. In the process of connecting plausible sentences, non-existent sources may be created, and if search is turned off, there is no basis for verification. Conversely, not knowing the latest events is due to the knowledge cutoff, and missing conditions in long conversations is due to the limits of the context window.

Since the three limits come from different places, their responses are also different. Baseline issues require retrieval and source verification, window limit issues require summarization and new dialogue, and generation method issues require direct verification. The fact that the tone is confident does not in any way guarantee accuracy.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: If you get a wrong answer, ask a question first. Was it after the reference date, was the conversation too long, or was it just made up?

checks.q: During a long conversation, you ask about a product announced yesterday. The model confidently gives incorrect specifications. Even with a context window of more than one million tokens, what is the most likely cause of this error?
options: This is because the first part was cut off because the combined limit of input and output was exceeded.
This is because the token was divided too finely and the specification number could not be read.
This is because events after the end of the training data cannot be reflected without tools.
This is because it is a stochastic generation, so the specifications change randomly every time a question is asked.
checks.explain: Events after the knowledge cutoff are unknown to the model without tools such as search. The size of the window is the amount it can contain, and the base date is the learning point, so they are different limits.

wrong.0: Window limit problems appear when long inputs pile up and conditions are missed, which is different from the reason we don't know the latest events.
wrong.1: Token splitting is only a matter of processing units and has nothing to do with whether you know the latest facts.
wrong.3: The probability of creation is the reason why sentences vary, not the reason we do not know the facts after the reference date.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: To get the same answer as close to 0 as possible with the model's API that supports temperature control, I lowered the temperature to as close to 0 as possible. What is the correct explanation?
options: It is guaranteed that the answer will always be the same down to the letter.
The candidate with the highest probability is almost always chosen, so the answers will be similar, but they are not guaranteed to be exactly the same.
Even the latest facts that are not in the training data are answered accurately.
You can change it in the same way in the settings screen of the chat app.
checks.explain: Lowering the temperature reduces bias by allowing high-probability candidates to be chosen more often, but as the document explains, the results are not completely conclusive. This setting is the value you specify in your API call.

wrong.0: The documentation tells us that even if the temperature is 0.0, the results are not completely conclusive.
wrong.2: Temperature only changes the way candidates are selected, but does not change the knowledge cutoff, which is the range of knowledge the model has.
wrong.3: These sampling settings are values specified in API calls and are usually not adjustable in chat apps.

checks.q: When I asked about the market size for the report, I received a number with source citations. Try putting the flow of checking this in the correct order.
items: Make sure the search tool is turned on and that there is a link to a web source in the response.
We believe that if there had been no search, the figures and citations could have been created from learned patterns.
Add evidence through search or deep research or open the link directly to check the content.
checks.explain: First, check whether there is a search and link to the source, and if not, suspect that it is a pattern-based creation, and finally add evidence or open the link directly to check.
checks.intro: Let’s check what we looked at earlier with one problem. There are no records or grading, so feel free to solve it.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

left: Misrepresenting the specifications of a recently announced product
Missing the conditions set late in a long conversation

glossary.def: A model is a processing unit that divides text, images, etc. into small pieces. In the Gemini model, approximately 4 characters equal 1 token.
This is the limit on the number of tokens that can be used for both input and output in a single request.
This is the end of model training data. Subsequent events will not be reflected in the response without tools such as search.
This is the phenomenon of making up untrue content or non-existent citations, research, or sources to make it plausible.
It is a model that goes through an internal thinking stage before coming up with an answer. Tokens used in thoughts are also counted toward usage.
This setting sharpens or flattens the probability distribution of the next token. Lowering it will make the answers similar, but it's not guaranteed to be exactly the same.

misconceptions.myth: If the model speaks confidently, it is correct.
misconceptions.fact: Tone and accuracy are two different things. Models can express high confidence even in incorrect answers, so important figures and citations should be verified with sources.

misconceptions.myth: The same question should always have the same answer.
misconceptions.fact: Because probability is involved in creation, sentences or numbers may vary for the same question. In models that support this, deviations can be reduced by settings such as temperature in the API, but it is difficult to guarantee that they are exactly the same. The fact that something has changed is not a malfunction in itself.

misconceptions.myth: When the context window is large, the knowledge cutoff problem also disappears.
misconceptions.fact: The window is the amount that can be stored at one time, and the base date is when learning is completed, so they are different limits. If you need up-to-date information, you should use the search tool, not expand the window.

misconceptions.myth: The model is designed to say that it doesn't know what it doesn't know.
misconceptions.fact: Models are trained to continue to the next token, and are often refined to fit an evaluation method that only recognizes correct answers, so they are generally inclined toward answering. You can reduce this gradient by allowing people to say they don't know or asking for evidence.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: A token is the unit through which a model processes input and output and is the basis for calculating usage.
The context window is limited to the extent that input and output can be used together, and beyond the knowledge cutoff, it cannot be known without tools.
The answer may vary each time because it is generated probabilistically, and a confident tone does not mean accuracy.
Hallucination responds based on whether it comes from a base date, window limit, or creation method.

Settings such as temperature only reduce deviation but do not guarantee perfect agreement, and the learning and evaluation structure makes the model more inclined to answer rather than say it does not know.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What numbers or quotations would be difficult to use in my work if I just used the AI's answers, and how do I check them?
